title: 論語 衛靈公第十五
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 15, 〈衛靈公〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 15 of the Analects, 衛靈公 Wèi Líng gōng, named, as every book is, from its first words — 'Duke Ling of Wei', the ruler who asked Confucius about drawing up troops for battle and was told the Master had never studied it; he left Wei the next day. The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Book 15 has 41 passages, most of them single sayings. It opens with the Master's company out of food in Chen and Zilu's angry question whether a gentleman is ever brought to such straits (15.1); then comes the 'one thread' that runs through all he knows (15.2), and Shun, who ruled by doing nothing but facing south with reverence (15.4). Here are the single word to live by — what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others (15.23); a man can make the Way great, not the Way the man (15.28); in teaching there are no kinds (15.38); and, when it comes to humaneness, not giving way even to one's teacher (15.35). It closes with the Master guiding a blind music master to his seat and naming everyone present (15.41). Each numbered passage begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text, and two cards (15.18–19, 15.22–23) hold two chapters each, because his edition prints them with no comment between. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
衛靈公問陳於孔子。
孔子對曰：「
俎豆之事，
則嘗聞之矣；
軍旅之事，
未之學也。」
明日遂行。

sentences.l:
Duke Ling of Wei asked Kongzi about battle array.
Kongzi replied: “The matters of stands and dishes —
of those I have at some time heard;
the matters of armies and troops —
those I have not yet learned.”
The next day he set off.
sentences.i: Duke Ling of Wei asked Kongzi how troops should be drawn up for battle. Kongzi replied: “Of sacrificial vessels and how they are set out I have heard something; of armies and campaigns I have made no study.” The next day he left.
sentences.n: The book is named 衛靈公 from its opening words; Zhu Xi's heading counts forty-one chapters (凡四十一章), and our numbers are his. (Ruan Yuan's 1816 text starts a new chapter at 在陳絶糧 in the next unit, so from there its numbers run one ahead of ours.) 衛靈公 Duke Ling of Wei is the misruling lord of 14.20. 陳 here is read zhèn, the word later written 陣 'battle array' (Zhu Xi: 陳去聲; 陳謂軍師行伍之列 'the ranks and files of an army'); He Yan's Kong Anguo: the method of drawing up an army in ranks. In the next unit the same graph is chén, the state of Chen. 對 is the formal 'replied', used to a superior. 俎 zǔ is a stand for meat offerings, 豆 a stemmed dish; together, Zhu Xi says, vessels of the rites (禮器), and so the rites themselves. Each half of the answer is a topic, 'the matters of…', then a comment: 則 'then, as for that'; 嘗 cháng 'once, at some time'. 未之學 'not yet it learned': after a negative such as 未, a pronoun object (之) comes before the verb. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 12,500 men make a 軍 and 500 a 旅; armies are a branch matter, and where the root is not yet established one cannot be taught the branches. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun (尹氏): Duke Ling was a lord without the Way, and on top of that had his mind on war and conquest, so the Master answered that he had not learned it, and left him. 遂 'thereupon'; 行 xíng 'to set out' — he left Wei.

sentences.t:
在陳，絶糧，
従者病，
莫能興。
sentences.i: In Chen their food ran out; his followers were so weak with hunger and sickness that none of them could stand.
sentences.n: 陳 chén is the state of Chen, south of Lu — the same graph as the zhèn 'battle array' just above. Zhu Xi: Kongzi left Wei and went to Chen. 絶 is the edition's form of 絕 jué 'to be cut off from, to be without'; 糧 liáng is grain, provisions for a journey. 従者 'those following', the disciples travelling with him: Zhu Xi marks 従 去聲 (zòng), the reading for an attendant; modern practice reads cóng, and so do we (as 11.2). 病 'ill, exhausted'. 莫能 'none could'; 興 xīng 'to rise' (Zhu Xi: 興起也). He Yan's Kong Anguo: 從者 are the disciples, and 興 is to rise; Kongzi left Wei for Cao, Cao would not receive him; he went on to Song and met the trouble with the men of Kuang (遭匡人之難); then he went to Chen, and when Wu attacked Chen, Chen was in disorder, and so they ran short of food. Ruan Yuan's 1816 text begins its 15.2 here.

sentences.t:
子路慍見曰：「
君子亦有窮乎？」
子曰：「
君子固窮，
小人窮斯濫矣。」

sentences.i: Zilu came to the Master smarting and said: “Does even a gentleman come to the end of his road?” The Master said: “Of course a gentleman comes to the end of his road at times. It is the small man who, once there, throws off all restraint.”
sentences.n: 慍 yùn 'resentful, aggrieved', as in 1.1. 見 is xiàn 'to come before, present oneself' (Zhu Xi: 賢遍反). 亦 'too' — the gentleman as well? 窮 qióng is to come to the end, to have no way through: the opposite of getting through (達). In the answer 固 can be taken two ways, and Zhu Xi gives both. He quotes a Mr He (何氏): 濫 is to overflow; the gentleman surely has his times of straits, unlike the small man, who in straits overflows and does wrong (放溢為非) — words that are, nearly verbatim, the unnamed comment in He Yan's collection. Then Master Cheng: 固窮 is 'holds firm in his straits' (固守其窮), which, Zhu Xi says, also works (亦通). 斯 'then'. Zhu Xi's own word: the sage goes when he should go, without misgivings, and in hardship comes through (處困而亨) without resentment or regret; this can be seen here, and learners should savour it deeply. Variant: He Yan's text reads 君子亦窮乎, without 有.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
賜也，
女以予為多學而識之者與？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Ci,
do you take me for one who learns much and keeps it in memory?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Ci, do you think of me as a man who has learned a great many things and remembers them all?”
sentences.n: 賜 Ci is Zigong's personal name (1.15), used by his teacher; 也 after a name in address is a calling pause. 女 is rǔ 'you' (Zhu Xi: 女音汝; He Yan's text writes 汝). 以X為Y 'take X to be Y'; 予 yú 'I, me'. 識 is zhì 'to remember, keep in mind' (Zhu Xi: 識音志), as in 7.2. The whole of 多學而識之 is closed by 者 'one who…'. 與 is yú, a question particle (Zhu Xi: 與平聲, and 'the same below', 下同). Zhu Xi: Zigong's learning was wide and he could remember it; the Master wanted him to know what it all rests on, so he asked, to draw him out.

sentences.t:
對曰：「
然，
非與？」
sentences.l:
He replied: “Yes.
Is it not so?”
sentences.i: “Yes,” he answered. “Is that not so?”
sentences.n: 然 'so it is, yes'. 非與 'is it not?' — 與 yú again the question particle. Zhu Xi: just as he was agreeing, he suddenly doubted — presumably because his long work at learning had brought him far, and he too was about to get something. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 然 means he did think him one who learns much and remembers; 非與 asks, 'Is it now not so?' (問今不然邪也).

sentences.t:
曰：「
非也，
予一以貫之。」
sentences.l:
He said: “No.
With me, one thing strings it through.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “No. There is one thing that runs through all of it.”
sentences.n: 非也 'it is not (so)'. 予一以貫之 'I, by one (thing), string it through': 一以 is 以一 'by means of one' with the object put first, as in 4.15 吾道一以貫之, whose English we keep. 貫 'to string together, run through' (Zhu Xi at 4.15: 通也). Zhu Xi: the saying is explained at Book 4; but there it is spoken of conduct, here of knowledge (彼以行言而此以知言也). He quotes Xie Liangzuo: the sage's Way is great and men cannot take it all in, so naturally they think it much learning and memory; but how should the sage be one who works at breadth? He is like Heaven with its many forms — it does not carve them thing by thing. Then two lines of the Odes: virtue is light as a hair, yet a hair still has its like; the doings of high Heaven have neither sound nor smell (德輶如毛，毛猶有倫；上天之載，無聲無臭) — 'that is the utmost'. And Yin Tun: to Master Zeng the Master said this straight out, without waiting to be asked, and Master Zeng understood it deeply and answered 'Yes' (4.15); with Zigong he first drew out the doubt and then told him, and Zigong never could answer 'Yes' as Master Zeng did — here the depth of the two men's learning can be seen. Zhu Xi adds that the Master often drew Zigong out in this way, and others had no part in it, so the depth of learning of the disciples below Yan Hui and Master Zeng can be seen as well. He Yan's comment (unnamed): good has its source and affairs their meeting point; the world has different roads but one destination, a hundred thoughts but one end (天下殊塗而同歸，百慮而一致); know the source and all the good is in hand — so there is no need of much learning: by one thing he knows it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
由！
知德者鮮矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Yóu!
Those who know virtue are few.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yóu, there are not many who understand virtue.”
sentences.n: 由 Yóu is Zilu's personal name (Zhu Xi: the Master calls Zilu by his name to tell him this), as in 2.17. 知德者 'those who know virtue': 者 closes the phrase. The edition prints 德 here and its usual 徳 elsewhere; the word is the same. 鮮 is xiǎn 'few' (Zhu Xi: 鮮上聲), and 矣 marks the state of things. Zhu Xi: 德 is what one has got of right and principle in oneself (義理之得於己者); unless one has it oneself, one cannot know its real savour. He adds that everything from the first chapter of the book to here was perhaps said at one time (自弟一章至此疑皆一時之言 — the print has 弟 for 第), and that this chapter was probably spoken because of Zilu's resentful appearance in 15.1. He Yan's Wang Su says the same: the gentleman is firm in straits, yet Zilu came before him resentful; so the Master told him there are few who know virtue.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
無為而治者，
其舜也與！
夫何為哉？
恭己正南面而已矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “One who governed well without doing anything —
that surely was Shun!
Now what did he do?
He made himself reverent and faced squarely south, and that was all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If ever a man kept the realm in order while doing nothing, it was Shun. And what did he do? He held himself in reverence and took his seat looking south — nothing more.”
sentences.n: The print has 恭已, a misprint for 恭己, corrected here. The Siku copy confuses 己 'oneself', 已 'to stop' and 巳 throughout (as at 4.14 and 5.15); Zhu Xi's own comment on the line has 恭己者聖人敬德之容, Ruan Yuan's 1816 text reads 恭己, and He Yan's text prints 巳, its form for both. 'Made himself reverent' is the only sense the line allows; the final 而已矣 'and that is all' is 已 yǐ, as printed. 無為而治者 'the one who, without doing, governed well' (為 wéi, 治 zhì): 者 closes the whole phrase. 其…也與 'surely it was…!' — 與 yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 夫 fú opens the question, 'now' (Zhu Xi: 音扶). 恭己 is verb and object, 'made himself reverent'; 南面 'to face south', the ruler's seat (6.1). Zhu Xi: governing without doing is the sage's virtue so abundant that the people are transformed without his needing to do anything. Shun alone is named because he came after Yao and also got the right men to fill all the offices, so still less trace of his doing is seen. 恭己 is the bearing of the sage reverent in virtue; since he did nothing, this was all that people saw. He Yan's comment (unnamed): he gave the offices to the right men, and so governed without doing.

sentences.t: 子張問行。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zizhang asked about getting through.
sentences.i: Zizhang asked how a man could make his way wherever he went.
sentences.n: 子張 Zizhang is Zhuansun Shi 顓孫師 (2.18). 行 xíng here is 'to go, to get through' — to have one's way and meet no block. Zhu Xi: it is like asking about 達 'making one's way' (猶問達之意也), the question Zizhang asks in 12.20.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
言忠信，
行篤敬，
雖蠻貊之邦，行矣；
言不忠信，
行不篤敬，
雖州里，行乎哉？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “In speech wholehearted and true to one's word,
in conduct solid and reverent —
even in the states of the Man and the Mo, one gets through;
in speech not wholehearted and true to one's word,
in conduct not solid and reverent —
even in one's own district and village, does one get through?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Let your words be wholehearted and true and your conduct steady and respectful, and you will find your way even among the tribes of the south and the north. If your words are not wholehearted and true, and your conduct not steady and respectful, will you find your way even in your own neighbourhood?”
sentences.n: Two halves of one shape: two conditions, then 雖 'even' + a place + 行 'gets through'. Zhu Xi marks the 行 of 行篤 and 行不 去聲, xìng, the noun 'conduct'; modern practice reads xíng, and so do we (as 14.4). The other two 行 are the verb of Zizhang's question, 'to get through'. 忠 'wholehearted' and 信 'good faith' are the pair of 1.4; 篤 is 'solid, thick' (Zhu Xi: 篤厚也), 敬 'reverent'. Zhu Xi: 蠻 mán are the Man of the south and 貊 mò (亡百反) the Di of the north (蠻南蠻貊北狄) — peoples outside the Chinese states. 州 zhōu and 里 are units of one's own home ground: Zhu Xi, 2,500 households make a 州; He Yan's Zheng Xuan, 12,500 households make a 州, and five households a 鄰, five 鄰 a 里. 行乎哉 'does one get through?' expects no — Zheng Xuan: it means one cannot. Zhu Xi: Zizhang's thought was of getting his way out in the world, so the Master turned him back to himself, as in his answers about seeking a salary (2.18) and making one's way (12.20).

sentences.t:
立則見其參於前也；
在輿則見其倚於衡也；
夫然後行。
sentences.i: When you stand, see them there in front of you; when you ride in your carriage, see them resting on the yoke before you. Only then will you get through.
sentences.n: The Master's answer runs on past Zhu Xi's comment and is left unquoted. 其 'them' — Zhu Xi: it points to the four things just named, wholeheartedness, good faith, solidity and reverence. 參 is read cān (Zhu Xi: 七南反); he says it is the 參 of the saying 'do not go and make a third' (母往參焉; the print has 母 for 毋), meaning they stand alongside one (與我相參也). 輿 yú is a carriage, and 衡 héng the crossbar of the yoke at the front (Zhu Xi: 衡軛也). 見 here is jiàn 'to see'. 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 音扶) opens the last clause: 'now, it being so, after that — one gets through'. Zhu Xi: one never forgets them in any thought; wherever one is, it is always as if one saw them; though one wished to leave them for a moment one could not; then every word and act will of itself not leave them, and one can get through even among the Man and the Mo. He Yan's Bao Xian: 衡 is the yoke; thinking always of wholeheartedness and good faith, standing, one seems to see them 'ranged' (參然) before one, and in the carriage, as if leaning on the yoke. Variant: He Yan's text reads 立則見其參然於前也 'ranged before one' and ends 夫然後行也, adding 也.

sentences.t: 子張書諸紳。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: Zizhang wrote it on his sash.
sentences.i: Zizhang wrote the saying on the end of his sash.
sentences.n: 諸 is the fused 之於 'it on'. 紳 shēn is the great sash of formal dress (10.13); Zhu Xi: the hanging end of the great sash (紳大帶之垂者), and he wrote it there because he wished not to forget it. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 紳 is the great sash. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: learning must press close in upon oneself; 'learn broadly and be firm in aim, ask closely and think of what is near' (19.6), and the Master's words here — 'in speech wholehearted and true, in conduct solid and reverent; standing, see them ranged before you; in the carriage, see them leaning on the yoke' — this is learning itself. One of fine stuff sees through it fully, the dregs melt away, and he becomes one body with Heaven and Earth; the next best keep and nourish it by gravity and reverence; when they arrive, it is one and the same.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
直哉史魚！
邦有道，如矢；
邦無道，如矢。」

morph.gloss: Shi Yu — the archivist Yu, a grandee of Wei

sentences.i: The Master said: “How straight Shi Yu was! When the state was well governed he went straight as an arrow, and when it was badly governed he went straight as an arrow still.”
sentences.n: 直哉史魚 'straight — how! — Shi Yu': in an exclamation the predicate comes first, as in 9.2 大哉孔子. Zhu Xi: 史 is the name of his office, the archivist; 魚 is a grandee of Wei, whose personal name was Qiu 鰌 (史官名，魚衛大夫名鰌); He Yan's Kong Anguo: the Wei grandee Shi Qiu (史鰌). 如矢 'like an arrow' — Zhu Xi: it means straight. He adds the story behind the praise: Shi Yu, because he had failed to bring forward the worthy and send away the unworthy, still remonstrated with his lord after death, by means of his corpse (尸諫); the affair is in the Kongzi jiayu (家語). Kong Anguo: whether the state had the Way or not, his conduct was straight as an arrow and did not bend.

sentences.t:
君子哉蘧伯玉！
邦有道，則仕；
邦無道，則可巻而懷之。

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
jade, the precious stone (有美玉於斯 'here is a fine jade')

sentences.i: And what a gentleman Qu Boyu was! When the state was well governed he took office; when it was badly governed he could fold away what he had to offer and keep it to himself.
sentences.n: The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment and are left unquoted. 君子哉 + name is the shape of 5.2 'A gentleman indeed, this man!'. 蘧伯玉 Qu Boyu is the grandee of Wei of 14.26. 仕 'to take office'. 巻 juǎn is the edition's form of 卷 'to roll up'; Zhu Xi: 巻收也 'to gather in', 懷藏也 'to store away'. 之 'it' is not named: whatever he had to give. 可 'could' — it was in his power to do so. Zhu Xi: Boyu's going out to serve and staying home both fitted the sage's Way, so he is called a gentleman; such was his giving no answer and leaving when Sun Linfu and Ning Zhi plotted the expulsion and murder of their rulers (如於孫林父甯殖放弑之謀不對而出亦其事也). He quotes Yang Shi: Shi Yu's straightness did not reach the whole of the gentleman's Way; only one like Qu Boyu could come through a disordered age unharmed — with Shi Yu's arrow-straightness, even had he wished to roll it up and put it away, he could not have. He Yan's Bao Xian: to roll up and put away means taking no part in the government of the day — yielding, and giving offence to no one. Variant: He Yan's text reads 可卷而懷也, with 也 for 之.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
可與言而不與之言，
失人；
不可與言而與之言，
失言。
知者不失人，
亦不失言。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “One who could be talked with, and you do not talk with him —
you lose the man;
one who could not be talked with, and you talk with him —
you lose your words.
The wise one loses no man,
and loses no words either.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man would repay your talking with him and you hold your tongue, you have lost him; if he would not and you talk to him anyway, your words are thrown away. One who is wise loses neither the man nor his words.”
sentences.n: 可與言 'can be talked with': 與 yǔ 'with', its object (the man) left unsaid; then 與之言 'talk with him', 之 'him'. Each half is a condition and a short verdict, 失人 'lose the man', 失言 'lose the words'. 知者 'the wise one', 知 zhì (Zhu Xi: 知去聲). Zhu Xi gives only the sound note here, and He Yan has no comment. Variants: Ruan Yuan's 1816 text reads 可與言而不與言, without 之; He Yan's text has the same, and in the second half 而與言之 'and talk with him', with 之 after the verb.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
志士，仁人，
無求生以害仁；
有殺身以成仁。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “No man of firm purpose, no humane man, will buy his life by doing harm to humaneness; there have been those who went to their deaths so that humaneness might be made whole.”
sentences.n: 志士 'an officer of purpose' — Zhu Xi: an officer who has a will set (有志之士); 仁人 'a humane man' — Zhu Xi: a man of completed virtue (成徳之人). The two are the topic; then 無… 'there are none who…' and 有… 'there are those who…'. 以 'so as to, and thereby'. 殺身 'to kill one's own person': 殺 shā, 身 'oneself'. Zhu Xi: when by principle one ought to die and yet seeks life, there is unease in one's heart — that harms the virtue of the heart; when one ought to die and dies, the heart is at ease and virtue is whole. He quotes Master Cheng: real principle, once got in the heart, is of itself different; real principle is truly seeing right as right and wrong as wrong; those of old who gave up their bodies and lost their lives could not have done it without truly seeing, and they must have seen that life is not weightier than what is right, and that living is not more at ease than dying; so 'there are those who kill themselves to complete humaneness' — it is only making one 'right' complete (成就一箇是而已). He Yan's Kong Anguo: they do not seek life and harm humaneness; they die, and so complete humaneness — the officer of purpose and the humane man do not cling to their own lives.

sentences.t:
子貢問為仁。
子曰：「
工欲善其事，
必先利其器。
居是邦也，
事其大夫之賢者，
友其士之仁者。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zigong asked about practising humaneness.
The Master said: “A craftsman who would make a good job of his work
must first put an edge on his tools.
Living in a given state,
serve the worthy among its grandees,
befriend the humane among its officers.”
sentences.i: Zigong asked how to go about being humane. The Master said: “A workman who means his work to turn out well sees first to the edge of his tools. In whatever state you live, take service with those of its grandees who are worthy, and make friends of those of its officers who are humane.”
sentences.n: 為仁 wéi rén 'practising humaneness' — Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: Zigong asked about practising humaneness, not about humaneness itself, so Kongzi told him only what one practises it with (為仁之資). 工 gōng is a craftsman. 善其事 'make his work good'; 利 'sharp' used as a verb, 'to sharpen'. 是邦 'this state' — whatever state one lives in. 大夫之賢者 'the worthy ones among the grandees', 士之仁者 'the humane ones among the officers': X之Y者 picks the Y ones out of X. Zhu Xi: 'worthy' is said with regard to affairs, 'humane' with regard to virtue; the Master once said that Zigong liked those not up to himself (悦不若己者), so he told him this, wishing him to have men to stand in awe of and to be cut and polished by (嚴憚切磋), and so to complete his virtue. He Yan's Kong Anguo: as the craftsman works with sharp tools, a man takes worthy friends as his help. Variant: He Yan's text ends 友其士之仁者也, adding 也.

sentences.t: 顔淵問為邦。

morph.gloss: = 顏 (the edition's form): Yan (a surname, in 顔淵)
Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.l: Yan Yuan asked about governing a state.
sentences.i: Yan Yuan asked how a state should be governed.
sentences.n: 顔淵 Yan Yuan is Yan Hui, the disciple the Master rated highest. 為邦 'governing a state', 為 wéi, as 13.11. Zhu Xi: Yanzi had the gifts of a king's chief helper (王佐之才), so he asked about the Way of ordering the world; saying 'a state' is the modest form of words (謙辭).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
行夏之時。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Use the seasons of the Xia.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Keep the calendar of the Xia.”
sentences.n: The answer comes in four short orders, each with Zhu Xi's comment after it; the next four units carry on the Master's words and are left unquoted. 行 xíng 'to put into use'. 夏 Xia is the first of the Three Dynasties; 時 'the seasons', the calendar. Zhu Xi: the Xia seasons take as the head of the year the month in which, at first dusk, the handle of the Dipper points to yin 寅. Heaven opened at zi 子, earth at chou 丑, man was born at yin 寅, so the months in which the handle points to any of these three could head the year, and the Three Dynasties used them in turn: the Xia took yin, man's standard; the Shang chou, earth's; the Zhou zi, Heaven's. But the seasons are for doing work, so the year should be reckoned by man. That is why Kongzi once said, 'I got the seasons of Xia' (吾得夏時焉), which expounders take to mean such works as the Xia xiaozheng (夏小正); he chose it for the rightness of its seasons and the goodness of its ordinances, and here told Yanzi the same. He Yan's comment (unnamed): it was based on seeing the birth of the ten thousand things, which it made the beginning of the four seasons, and he chose it because it is easy to know.

sentences.t: 乘殷之輅。
sentences.l: Ride the state carriage of the Yin.
sentences.i: Ride in the carriage of the Yin.
sentences.n: 乘 is chéng 'to ride' here, not shèng 'a chariot'. 殷 Yin is the Shang dynasty. 輅 lù is a great carriage (Zhu Xi: 輅音路, also written 路). Zhu Xi: the Shang carriage was a wooden one; 輅 is the name of the great carriage; in antiquity carriages were simply made of wood, and the name 輅 appears with the Shang, which perhaps first gave it a distinct form. The Zhou decorated theirs with gold and jade, which was too lavish and easily spoiled — not as good as the Shang carriage, plain, whole and solid, while rank was already marked: substance, and the mean struck. He Yan's Ma Rong: the Yin carriage was called the Great Lu (大輅), and the Zuo zhuan's 'the Great Lu, with rush matting' (大輅越席) shows its frugality.

sentences.t: 服周之冕。
sentences.l: Wear the ceremonial cap of the Zhou.
sentences.i: Wear the ceremonial cap of the Zhou.
sentences.n: 服 'clothes', used as a verb, 'to wear'. 冕 is the ceremonial cap, as in 9.3. Zhu Xi: the Zhou had five kinds of 冕, the caps of sacrificial dress, with a board on top and strings of pendants front and back; something of the kind had existed since the Yellow Emperor, but its rules and grades were first complete under the Zhou. Yet it is a small thing set above the whole body, so though ornate it is not wasteful and though costly not extravagant; the Master chose it, perhaps, as pattern that strikes the mean. He Yan's Bao Xian: the 冕 is the cap of the rites; the Zhou rites were patterned and complete; and it was chosen for its yellow silk-floss ear-stoppers (黈纊塞耳), not giving free rein to eyes and ears (不任視聴).

sentences.t: 樂則韶舞。
sentences.l: For music, the Shao and its dances.
sentences.i: For music, the Shao of Shun, with its dances.
sentences.n: 樂 is yuè 'music'. 則 after a topic: 'as for music, then…'. 韶 the Shao is the music of Shun (3.25, 7.13); 舞 'dance' — music and dance went together in performance. Zhu Xi: he chose it for being wholly good and wholly beautiful (取其盡善盡美), the words of 3.25. He Yan's comment (unnamed): the Shao is Shun's music, wholly good and wholly beautiful, so he chose it.

sentences.t:
放鄭聲，
逺佞人。
鄭聲淫，
佞人殆。
sentences.l:
Banish the sounds of Zheng,
keep glib men far away:
the sounds of Zheng run to excess,
glib men are a danger.
sentences.i: Ban the music of Zheng and keep smooth talkers at a distance. The music of Zheng leads to excess, and smooth talkers are a danger.
sentences.n: Two orders, then the reason for each. 放 is 'to banish' — Zhu Xi: to forbid and cut it off (禁絶之). 鄭聲 'the sounds of Zheng', Zhu Xi: the music of the state of Zheng. 逺 is the edition's form of 遠, here the verb 'to keep at a distance'; Zhu Xi marks it 去聲, yuàn, a reading modern practice does not keep (we print yuǎn). 佞人 Zhu Xi: men low, fawning and glib (卑諂辯給之人); 殆 'dangerous' (Zhu Xi: 殆危也). Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: many asked about government, but only to Yan Yuan did the Master answer like this; the institutions of the Three Dynasties each added and cut according to the times, and in time could not be free of faults; with the Zhou in decline and no sage arising, Kongzi weighed the rites of the former kings and set up a Way to be practised for ten thousand ages, giving this as its outline — from it the rest can be worked out. Zhang Zai: rites and music are the method of ordering; banishing the Zheng sounds and keeping glib men away is the intent beyond the method — one day's carelessness, and the method is broken; and again: when a method is set up and can be kept, virtue can last and the work grow great, and Zheng sounds and glib men can make men lose what they keep, so they must be banished and kept away. Yin Tun: this is the great method no king in a hundred could change; Kongzi's making of the Chunqiu was perhaps in this spirit; though Kongzi and Yan Hui could not put it into practice in their day, their method of order can still be seen. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Zheng sounds and glib men can move men's hearts just as elegant music and worthy men do, but they bring men to excess, disorder and danger; therefore they must be banished and kept away.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
人無逺慮，
必有近憂。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A man with no thought that reaches far
is sure to have cares close by.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man's foresight does not reach far, trouble will soon be at his elbow.”
sentences.n: 逺 yuǎn 'far' (the edition's form of 遠) is here an adjective, 'far-reaching', set against 近 'near'. 無X，必有Y 'without X, (he) surely has Y'. Zhu Xi quotes Su (蘇氏): of the ground a man treads on, all beyond the room for his feet is useless, yet it cannot be done away with; so if thought does not reach beyond a thousand li, trouble lies under the table and mat (几席之下). He Yan has no comment. Variant: He Yan's text reads 人而無逺慮 'a man, if without far thought', with 而.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
已矣乎！
吾未見好徳如好色者也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “It is finished!
I have not yet seen one delighting in virtue as he delights in beauty.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “There is no hope of it. Never yet have I met a man who cared for virtue the way men care for a pretty face.”
sentences.n: The second line is 9.17 word for word, and its English is kept; the cry before it is the 已矣乎 'it is finished!' of 5.26. 已 yǐ 'to stop, be over'; 矣 and 乎 make it an exclamation. 好 is hào 'to be fond of' both times (Zhu Xi: 好去聲); 徳 is the edition's form of 德. Zhu Xi: 已矣乎 sighs that in the end he will never get to see it. He Yan has no comment here.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
臧文仲其竊位者與！
知栁下惠之賢而不與立也。」

morph.gloss: Zang (the Zangsun house of Lu, in 臧文仲)
Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu
Liuxia Hui — Zhan Huo, a grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Zang Wenzhong — surely one who stole his post!
He knew Liuxia Hui's worth, and yet did not stand with him.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Zang Wenzhong held his office like a thief. He knew what Liuxia Hui was worth, yet never brought him to stand beside him at court.”
sentences.n: 臧文仲 Zang Wenzhong is the grandee of Lu of 5.17. 其…者與 'surely (he is) one who…!': 其 'surely', 與 yú (Zhu Xi: 者與之與平聲). 竊位 'to steal a post' — Zhu Xi: one not fit for his post and ashamed of it in his heart, like a thief who has got something and holds it in secret. 栁 is the edition's form of 柳 liǔ. Zhu Xi: Liuxia Hui was a grandee of Lu, Zhan Huo 展獲, courtesy name Qin 禽; his fief was Liuxia, and his posthumous name Hui (栁下惠魯大夫展獲字禽食邑栁下諡曰惠). 與立 'stand with', 與 yǔ — Zhu Xi: to stand side by side with him at court. He quotes Fan Zuyu: Zang Wenzhong governed Lu; not to know the worthy is a failure of sight, to know them and not raise them is to keep the worthy hidden; the first is the smaller fault, the second the greater; so Kongzi called him not humane, and also a stealer of his post. He Yan's Kong Anguo: Liuxia Hui is Zhan Qin; knowing he was worthy and not raising him is stealing a post.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
躬自厚而薄責於人，
則逺怨矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Heavy on one's own self, and light in blaming others —
then one keeps resentment far off.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Lay the heavy blame on yourself and only light blame on others, and no one will bear you a grudge.”
sentences.n: 躬 'one's own person' and 自 'oneself' stress the self; 厚 'heavy, thick' and 薄 'thin, light' are the pair. 責 zé 'to blame, to demand of' is written once and serves both halves: Zhu Xi reads the first as 'blaming oneself heavily' (責己厚) and the second as 'blaming others lightly' (責人薄). 則 'then'. 逺 here is again the verb 'to keep at a distance', which Zhu Xi marks 去聲 (yuàn); we print the modern yuǎn, as at 15.10. Zhu Xi: blaming himself heavily, his own person is the better cultivated; blaming others lightly, others find it easy to follow him; and so they cannot resent him. He Yan's Kong Anguo: to blame oneself heavily and others lightly is the way to keep resentment and blame (怨咎) far away.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不曰『如之何，如之何』者，
吾末如之何也已矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “One who does not say ‘What to do about it? What to do about it?’ —
with him I have no way of doing anything, and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man never asks himself ‘What should I do about this? What should I do?’, I am at a loss what to do about him.”
sentences.n: 如之何 'what to do about it?' is the bound phrase of 9.23, used twice as the words a man might say and once as the Master's own; the closing 吾末如之何也已矣 is 9.23's, and its English is kept. 末 mò 'no, there is no way' (= 無). The whole of 不曰…者 'one who does not say…' is the topic. Zhu Xi: 'what to do about it, what to do about it' are the words of one who thinks a thing through and weighs how to handle it (熟思而審處之辭); one who does not, and acts recklessly — even a sage can do nothing with him. He Yan's Kong Anguo: not saying 如之何 is like not saying 'what can be done about this?' (奈是何); and on the last words: when calamity has already taken shape, I too can do nothing about it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
羣居終日，
言不及義，
好行小慧，
難矣哉！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Together in a crowd the whole day,
their talk never reaching what is right,
fond of practising petty cleverness —
hard indeed!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A pack of people who spend all day together, whose talk never touches on what is right, and who love to show off their little tricks of wit — it is hard to make anything of them!”
sentences.n: 羣 qún is the edition's form of 群 'a herd, a crowd'; 羣居 'to stay together in a crowd'. 終日 'the whole day'. 及 'to reach'. 好 is hào 'to be fond of' (Zhu Xi: 好去聲). 小慧 'petty cleverness' — Zhu Xi: private cleverness (私智); He Yan's Zheng Xuan: small talents and wits. 難矣哉 'hard — how!'. Zhu Xi: when talk does not reach what is right, the heart of licence, perversity, depravity and extravagance (放辟邪侈) grows; when one is fond of petty cleverness, the springs of walking in danger and trusting to luck (行險僥倖) run hot; 難矣哉 says they have no way into virtue and harm is coming to them. Zheng Xuan: 難矣哉 means they will never achieve anything.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子義以為質，
禮以行之，
孫以出之，
信以成之。
君子哉！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman takes what is right as his substance,
carries it out by the rites,
brings it forth with humility,
completes it with good faith.
A gentleman indeed!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman makes what is right the stuff he is made of; he puts it into practice through the rites, brings it out with modesty, and sees it through with good faith. That is a gentleman!”
sentences.n: Four clauses of one shape: a noun put first, then 以 'by it' and a verb. 義以為質 is 以義為質 'takes right as substance' with the object brought forward; 禮以行之 is 以禮行之 'by the rites carries it out', and so on. 之 'it' each time is what is right. 質 'plain stuff, substance' (6.16) — Zhu Xi: the trunk (質幹). 行 xíng 'to carry out'. 孫 is xùn, the same word as 遜 'humble, yielding' (Zhu Xi: 孫去聲; He Yan's text writes 遜), as in 14.4. Zhu Xi: what is right is the root of dealing with affairs, so it is the trunk; carrying it out must have measure and pattern; bringing it out must be with modest yielding; completing it must lie in sincerity — that is the gentleman's Way. He quotes Master Cheng: 'right as substance' is like a trunk; the rites carry it out, humility brings it out, good faith completes it; the four lines are one thing only, with right as the root. And again: with reverence straighten the inner, then with right square the outer (敬以直内則義以方外); with right as substance, then the rites to carry it out, humility to bring it out, good faith to complete it. 君子哉 'a gentleman — indeed!' closes with the exclamation of 15.6. He Yan has no comment.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子病無能焉，
不病人之不己知也。」
子曰：「
君子疾没世而名不稱焉。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
(makes 'others do not know him' into a noun phrase)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman is troubled that he lacks ability, not that others do not know him.” The Master said: “The gentleman would be pained to reach the end of his days with nothing said of his name.”
sentences.n: This card holds two chapters, 15.18 and 15.19, which the edition prints with only a ○ between them and no commentary on the first; Zhu Xi's comment follows the second. 15.18: 病 is 'to be troubled by, to find oneself short'; what the gentleman finds lacking is in himself, 無能 'having no ability'; 焉 is a final particle. The second half is 1.16's first line made into a statement about the gentleman, and keeps its English: 之 makes 人之不己知 one noun phrase, 'others' not knowing him', and after the negative 不 the pronoun object 己 stands before the verb 知 zhī. Commenting on 14.32, Zhu Xi notes that this saying turns up four times in the book (by our count 1.16, 4.14, 14.32 and here), each time in different words, so the sage must have said it often (此章凡四見而文皆有異). 15.19: 疾 jí 'to be pained at, to hate'; He Yan's own comment: 疾猶病也 '疾 is like 病', so the two chapters use near-synonyms. 没世 'to come to the end of one's lifetime': 没 mò is the edition's form of 沒 (cf. 14.10 没齒 'to the end of his years'). 而 adds the second circumstance, 名不稱 'his name not spoken of' (稱 chēng). Zhu Xi quotes Fan Zuyu: the gentleman learns for his own sake and does not seek to be known by others; yet if to the end of his life his name is never spoken of, one can tell that there was no real doing of good in him (然没世而名不稱焉則無為善之實可知矣).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子求諸己，
小人求諸人。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman seeks it in himself;
the small man seeks it in others.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman looks to himself; the small man looks to other people.”
sentences.n: Two halves of one build, the gentleman set against the small man. 諸 zhū is the fused form of 之於 'it in': 求諸己 'seek it in oneself'. What 'it' is, the line leaves open. Zhu Xi quotes Xie Liangzuo: the gentleman in everything turns back and seeks it in himself, the small man does the opposite, and this is what divides them (此君子小人所以分也). He then quotes Yang Shi, who reads 15.18–20 together: though the gentleman is not troubled that others do not know him, he is still pained if his name goes unspoken to the end of his life; and though pained at that, what he seeks he still seeks only in himself; the small man seeks in others, and so goes against the Way to court praise and stops at nothing (違道干譽無所不至). The three sayings, Yang Shi says, do not share their wording but complete one another in sense, and that too was the recorder's intention (三者文不相蒙而義實相足亦記言者之意). He Yan's own comment: the gentleman makes demands of himself, the small man of others (君子責己小人責人也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子矜而不爭，
羣而不黨。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is grave but does not contend,
sociable but forms no faction.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman carries himself with dignity but picks no quarrels; he gets on with everyone but belongs to no faction.”
sentences.n: Two pairs of the shape A而不B 'A but not B': each quality is kept from sliding into its fault. 矜 jīn is 'grave, dignified' here (Bao Xian in He Yan: 矜矜莊也), not 'proud'; 爭 zhēng 'to contend, to quarrel'; 羣 qún (the edition's form of 群) is 'to flock together', so 'to keep company with others'; 黨 dǎng 'to form a faction, to side with one's own' (as 7.30 君子不黨). Zhu Xi: holding oneself with gravity is called 矜, but there is no contrary, quarrelsome heart, so he does not contend; dealing with the many at ease is called 羣, but there is no intent of fawning or cliquing, so he forms no faction (和以處衆曰羣然無阿比之意故不黨). Compare 3.7 君子無所争 and 2.14 周而不比. Kong Anguo in He Yan: 黨 is 'to help (one's own)'; gentlemen, though many, do not help one another privately, but side with what is right (義之與比, the words of 4.10).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子不以言舉人，
不以人廢言。」
子貢問曰：「
有一言而可以終身行之者乎？」
子曰：「
其恕乎！
己所不欲，
勿施於人。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman does not raise up a man for his words,
nor set aside words for the man.”
Zigong asked, saying: “Is there one saying that one can practise to the end of one's life?”
The Master said: “Surely it is fellow-feeling!
What you yourself do not want,
do not put upon others.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman does not promote a man because he speaks well, nor discard what a man says because of who he is.” Zigong asked: “Is there a single saying one could live by all one's life?” The Master said: “Fellow-feeling, surely. Anything you would not wish for yourself, do not lay on anyone else.”
sentences.n: This card holds two chapters, 15.22 and 15.23, which the edition prints with only a ○ between them and no commentary on the first; Zhu Xi's comment follows the second. 15.22: two matched clauses with 以 'because of': 以言舉人 'because of words, raise a man up', 以人廢言 'because of the man, set aside words'. 舉 is to raise up, to put forward for office (as 2.19 舉直); 廢 'to cast aside'. Zhu Xi has no comment on it; Bao Xian in He Yan: one who has (fine) words does not necessarily have virtue (有言者不必有徳, the Master's own words at 14.5), so one cannot raise a man up for his words. 15.23: 一言 'one saying' (as 13.15); 而可以 'and by it one can'; 終身 'to the end of one's life'; 行 xíng 'to practise'; 者 makes the whole question a thing, '(a saying) that…'. 其…乎 is a confident guess, 'surely it is…!'. 恕 shù 'fellow-feeling' is the second half of 4.15's 忠恕, where Zhu Xi defines it as extending oneself (推己之謂恕). The rule that follows is 12.2's and keeps its English: 己 'oneself' is the subject of the 所-phrase, and the whole 己所不欲 is the fronted object of 施 'to put upon'. Zhu Xi: extend oneself to reach others, and the use of it never runs out, so one can practise it all one's life (推己及物其施不窮故可以終身行之). He quotes Yin Tun: in learning what matters is to know the essential, and Zigong's question shows he knew it; Confucius told him the method of seeking humaneness (求仁之方; cf. 6.28); pushed to its limit, even the sage's selflessness does not go beyond this. Compare 5.11, where Zigong claims much the same rule for himself and the Master tells him he has not reached it. Variants: He Yan's text reads 可以終身行者乎 (no 之) and ends 勿施於人也 (a closing 也 added).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾之於人也，
誰毁誰譽？
如有所譽者，
其有所試矣。」

morph.gloss: (joins 'I' and 'with others' into one topic phrase)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “I, in my dealings with others —
whom have I disparaged, whom have I praised?
If there is someone I have praised,
surely there has been something he was tested by.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “In my dealings with people, whom have I run down, whom have I puffed up? If I have praised anyone, it is because he has already been put to some test.”
sentences.n: 吾之於人也 'I, in relation to others': 之 sets the subject 吾 together with 於人 as one topic phrase, and 也 pauses on it. 誰毁誰譽 'whom disparage, whom praise?': the question word 誰, the object, stands before each verb. 毁 huǐ 'to disparage, to run down'; 譽 'to praise' — Zhu Xi marks it 平聲, the old reading yú; we give the modern yù. Zhu Xi: to disparage is to speak of a man's faults so as to take away from the truth about him (稱人之惡而損其真), to praise is to raise up his good points beyond the facts (揚人之善而過其實), and the Master did neither; yet if there was someone he praised, he must already have tested him somehow and known how he would turn out. The sage, he says, is quick to approve the good, yet careless in nothing; slower to condemn the bad, so that even where he could know a man's badness beforehand, in the end he disparages no one. 所譽者 'the one whom (I) praise': 所 before a verb makes 'that which, the one whom'. 其有所試矣 'surely there has been something he was tested by': 其 marks a confident judgement. Bao Xian in He Yan: whom he praised he at once tested with some task; he did not praise emptily (所譽輙試以事不空譽而巳矣). The Master's words run on past Zhu Xi's comment; the next unit is left unquoted. Variant: He Yan's text reads 如有可譽者 'if there is one who can be praised' (可 for 所).

sentences.t:
斯民也，
三代之所以直道而行也。
sentences.l:
These people —
they are the ones through whom the Three Dynasties went by the straight way.
sentences.i: These people are the very ones with whom the Three Dynasties kept to the straight road.
sentences.n: Still the Master, unquoted. 斯民也 'these people': 斯 'this, these', 也 pausing on the topic. 三代 sān dài 'the Three Dynasties', Xia, Shang and Zhou (Zhu Xi: 三代夏商周也; Ma Rong in He Yan writes 夏殷周, Yin being another name for Shang). 所以 'that by which': 三代之所以直道而行 'that by which the Three Dynasties went by the straight way', made one noun phrase by 之 and standing as the predicate of 斯民. 直道 'the straight way' is, in Zhu Xi's words, having no private crookedness (無私曲也). Zhu Xi: 斯民 are the people of the present day; the Master means that the reason he neither disparages nor praises is that these are the very people with whom, in the age of the Three Dynasties, the good were treated as good and the bad as bad without private bias, so that he too cannot now twist the truth of their right and wrong (故我今亦不得而枉其是非之實也). He quotes Yin Tun: how would Confucius have any wish to disparage or praise? Where he praised, it was because he had tested a man and knew his worth; these people are those with whom the Three Dynasties went by the straight way — how could he let private feeling in between? Ma Rong in He Yan: the Three Dynasties employed the people like this, without partiality, which is why it is said they went by the straight way (用民如此無所阿私所以云直道而行也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
吾猶及史之闕文也。
有馬者借人乗之，
今亡已夫！」

morph.gloss: (makes 'a scribe leaves gaps in the text' one phrase)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “I still reached the time of scribes leaving gaps in the text.
One who had a horse lent it to others to ride.
Now there is none — it is over, alas!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I was still in time to see scribes leave a blank where they were unsure, and men who had a horse lend it to someone else to ride. Now all that is gone.”
sentences.n: 猶及 'still reached (in time for)': the Master was born early enough to see these things. 史之闕文 'a scribe's leaving gaps in the text': 之 makes 'the scribe leaves gaps in the writing' one phrase; 闕 quē is 'to leave a gap, to leave out' (as 2.18 多聞闕疑); 史 is the scribe who keeps records. 有馬者 'one who had a horse'; 借人乗之 'lent (it to) others to ride it' (借 jiè; 乗 chéng 'to ride', the edition's form of 乘). 亡 wú is 無 'there is none'; 已 yǐ 'it is over', and 夫 fú (Zhu Xi: 夫音扶) ends the sentence with a sigh. Zhu Xi does not explain the two things himself. He quotes Yang Shi: the scribe leaving gaps and the horse lent to others — these two things Confucius still lived to see; 'now there are none' grieves that the times were growing ever more slack (悼時之益偷也). Zhu Xi adds that this must have been said with something in view: trifling matters though they are, the great change of the times can be known from them. And he quotes Hu Yin: the sense of this chapter is doubtful and cannot be forced (此章義疑不可强解). Bao Xian in He Yan explains both: the scribes of old, in doubt over a character in a document, left it out to wait for one who knew (古之史於書字有疑則闕之以待知者也); one who had a horse he could not train well lent it to others to break in (使習之); Confucius says he himself lived to see such men, and now there are none — he says this because the custom of the day was much given to forced invention (以俗多穿鑿也). Variant: Ruan's text reads 今亡矣夫 and He Yan's 今則亡矣夫 ('now (then) there are none, alas'); Zhu Xi's text, and Yang Shi's comment quoting it, have 已夫. We keep 已, read yǐ.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
巧言亂徳。
小不忍，
則亂大謀。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Clever words throw virtue into disorder.
Not bearing small things —
then one throws great plans into disorder.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Smooth talk unsettles virtue. Lose patience over small things, and you will upset great plans.”
sentences.n: 巧言 'clever words', as in 1.3, where it stands with 令色. 亂 luàn 'disorder' is a verb here, 'to throw into disorder'; 徳 is the edition's form of 德. 小不忍 'in small things not bearing': 忍 is 'to bear, to endure, to bring oneself to'; 則 'then' gives the consequence, 亂大謀 'throw great plans into disorder'. Zhu Xi: clever words turn right and wrong upside down (巧言變亂是非), and whoever listens to them loses what he holds to; 'not bearing small things' covers both a woman's soft-heartedness and a common fellow's bravado (如婦人之仁匹夫之勇皆是). Kong Anguo in He Yan: clever words and a sharp tongue (巧言利口) throw virtue and right into disorder. Variant: He Yan's text lacks 則 (小不忍亂大謀).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
衆惡之，
必察焉；
衆好之，
必察焉。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The many hate him —
one must look into it;
the many love him —
one must look into it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When everyone hates a man, look into it for yourself; when everyone loves him, look into it for yourself.”
sentences.n: Two clauses of one shape: the condition is simply stated, 'the many hate him', then 必察焉 'one must examine (it)'. 衆 is the edition's form of 眾, 'the many, everyone'. 惡 wù 'to hate', 好 hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 好惡並去聲). 之 'him' is the man liked or hated; 焉 is 'into it' (the fused 於之). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: only the humane can love and hate people (4.3); if the many love or hate a man and one does not examine it, one may be blinded by partiality (衆好惡之而不察則或蔽於私矣). Wang Su in He Yan: sometimes the many are a clique sticking together (阿黨比周), sometimes the man stands alone and apart from the herd (特立不群), so their liking and hating must be examined. Compare 13.24, where the Master will not judge a man by his whole district's liking or hating either.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
人能𢎞道，
非道𢎞人。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A man can make the Way great;
it is not the Way that makes a man great.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It is people who can widen the Way and make it great; the Way does not do that for people.”
sentences.n: 𢎞 is the edition's form of 弘 hóng 'broad' (8.7 士不可以不𢎞毅), here a verb: Zhu Xi, 'to open it out and make it great' (𢎞廓而大之也). 非 'it is not (that)' denies the reversed sentence. Zhu Xi: there is no Way apart from man and no man apart from the Way; but the human heart is aware, while the Way in its substance does nothing (道體無為), so man can make his Way great and the Way cannot make its man great. He quotes Zhang Zai: the heart can fully realize the nature — that is man making the Way great; the nature does not know to check its heart — that is 'not the Way making man great'. He Yan's own comment: where the talent is great the Way follows it in greatness, where small it follows it in smallness, so (the Way) cannot make a man great (材大者道随大材小者道随小故不能弘人也). Variant: He Yan's text ends 非道弘人也, with a closing 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
過而不改，
是謂過矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “To err and not correct it —
this is what is called erring.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A fault you will not put right — that is the fault that counts.”
sentences.n: 過 'to go past the mark, to err' is the word of 1.8 過則勿憚改 'if you err, do not shrink from correcting it'. 是謂 'this is called': 是 'this' sums up the clause before it, and 矣 marks the verdict. Zhu Xi: if one errs and can correct it, one comes back to having no fault; only if one does not correct it does the fault become fixed, and soon it will be too late to correct (唯不改則其過遂成而將不及改矣). He Yan has no comment on the chapter.

sentences.t:
子曰：
吾嘗終日不食，
終夜不寢，
以思，
sentences.l:
The Master said: I once went a whole day without eating,
a whole night without sleeping,
to think:
sentences.i: The Master said: I once went all day without food and all night without sleep, so as to think;
sentences.n: Zhu Xi marks this sentence twice with (句) 'the phrase ends here', after 以思 and after 無益, and the units follow his marks; the Master's words are left without quotation marks across the three, as at 7.6. The marks keep 以思 with what goes before ('…in order to think') and make 無益 a clause of its own. 嘗 'once, at one time'. 終日 'the whole day', 終夜 'the whole night': 終 'to the end of'. 食 shí 'to eat'; 寢 qǐn 'to lie down to sleep'. 以思 'in order to think': 以 introduces the purpose.

sentences.t: 無益，
sentences.l: there was no gain;
sentences.i: and it did me no good;
sentences.n: The second of Zhu Xi's (句) marks closes this two-character clause. 無益 'no gain, no benefit': 益 is 'to add, to increase', and so 'profit'. He Yan's text runs the sentence on without a break and has no commentary on this chapter.

sentences.t: 不如學也。
sentences.l: it was not as good as learning.
sentences.i: I would have done better to learn.
sentences.n: 不如 'is not as good as' (as 13.24): thinking alone was not the equal of learning. Zhu Xi: this is said for those who think without learning; wearing out the mind to force an answer is not as good as humbling one's aim and gaining it of oneself (勞心以必求不如遜志而自得也). He quotes a Mr Li (李氏): the Master was not one who thought without learning; he only let these words fall to teach others (特垂語以教人爾). Compare 2.15: 'thinking and not learning — then in danger'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子謀道不謀食。
耕也，餒在其中矣；
學也，禄在其中矣。
君子憂道不憂貧。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman lays plans for the Way, not for food.
Ploughing — hunger is there within it;
learning — the salary is there within it.
The gentleman worries about the Way, not about being poor.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What the gentleman sets himself to win is the Way, not his food. A man may plough and still go hungry; a man may learn, and the salary will come of itself. What the gentleman worries about is the Way, not poverty.”
sentences.n: Two matching sentences about the gentleman frame a pair about ploughing and learning. 謀 'to plan for, to work at getting'; 食 shí 'food, eating'. 耕也 and 學也: 也 pauses on a topic, 'as for ploughing… as for learning…'. 耕 gēng 'to plough'; 餒 něi 'hunger' (Zhu Xi: 奴罪反; Zheng Xuan in He Yan: 餒餓也). 在其中矣 'is there within it' is the phrase, and the English, of 2.18 禄在其中矣. Zhu Xi: ploughing is the way to seek food, yet one may not get food; learning is the way to seek the Way, and the salary is in it; yet in learning one worries only about not attaining the Way — it is not from worry over poverty that one wants to do this and get a salary. He quotes Yin Tun: the gentleman tends the root and does not fret over the branch tips; how would he make outward things his worry or his joy? Zheng Xuan reads the middle lines as encouragement: a man who thinks of ploughing and does not learn goes hungry; one who learns gets a salary and, though he does not plough, does not go hungry — it urges people to learn (勸人學也). Variant: He Yan's text ends 不憂貧也, with a closing 也.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
知及之，
仁不能守之；
雖得之，
必失之。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Understanding reaches it,
humaneness cannot keep it:
though one gets it,
one will surely lose it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man's understanding is enough to reach it but his humaneness is not enough to hold it, then whatever he gains he is sure to lose.”
sentences.n: 知 is zhì, 'knowing, understanding' (Zhu Xi: 知去聲), the faculty set against the virtue 仁 'humaneness'. 及 'to reach'; 守 'to keep, to hold fast'; 雖 'though'; 必 'surely'. Each 之 is 'it', and the line does not say what it is. Zhu Xi takes it as the principle (理): understanding is enough to know this principle, but if selfish desires come between, one has no way to keep it in one's own person (知足以知此理而私欲間之則無以有之於身矣). Bao Xian in He Yan takes it as office: one whose knowledge reaches to governing his post but whose humaneness cannot hold it will surely lose it, though he gets it (知能及治其官而仁不能守雖得之必失之也). The chapter runs on past two more of Zhu Xi's comments; those units are left unquoted.

sentences.t:
知及之，
仁能守之，
不莊以涖之，
則民不敬。
sentences.i: If his understanding reaches it and his humaneness can hold it, but he does not come before the people with dignity, they will not respect him.
sentences.n: Still the Master, unquoted. The first two clauses repeat the last unit's, with 能 'can' for 不能. 莊 zhuāng 'grave, dignified' (as 2.20 臨之以莊); 以 links the manner to the verb: 'with gravity, thereby to oversee'. 涖 lì 'to come down to, to oversee': Zhu Xi, 涖 is 臨 'to look down on, to govern', meaning to oversee the people (涖臨也謂臨民也); so this 之 is 'them', the people. Zhu Xi: one who knows the principle with no selfish desires between keeps what he knows; yet some still lack gravity — a bias of temperament and habit, rich within but not stern without — so the people see nothing in him to stand in awe of, and they slight him (民不見其可畏而慢易之). Bao Xian in He Yan: if he does not oversee them with sternness, the people will not respect and follow those above (不嚴以臨之則民不敬從上也).

sentences.t:
知及之，
仁能守之，
莊以涖之，
動之不以禮，
未善也。
sentences.l:
Understanding reaches it,
humaneness can keep it,
with gravity one oversees them;
moving them not by the rites —
it is not yet good.
sentences.i: If his understanding reaches it, his humaneness can hold it and he comes before the people with dignity, but he does not stir them to act by the rites, it is still not good.
sentences.n: Still unquoted. Three clauses now hold, and the fourth names what is still missing. 動之 'to move them', the people; 不以禮 'not by means of the rites'. 未善 'not yet good'. Zhu Xi: 動之 is moving the people, like saying to drum them up and rouse them (猶曰鼓舞而作興之云爾); 禮 means the measured forms of right principle (義理之節文). His own judgement: when learning reaches humaneness, goodness is in oneself and the great root is set; overseeing without gravity and moving without the rites are small flaws of endowment or of learning, yet still not the way of complete goodness; so the Master went through them one by one, to show that the more complete the virtue, the more is asked of it, and these must not be slighted as small matters (不可以為小節而忽之也). Wang Su in He Yan: in moving them one must use the rites; only then is it good (動必以禮然後善也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子不可小知而可大受也；
小人不可大受而可小知也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman cannot be known through small things, but can take on great ones;
the small man cannot take on great things, but can be known through small ones.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “You cannot tell what a gentleman is from small matters, but he can be trusted with great ones. A small man cannot be trusted with great matters, but in small ones you can see what he is good for.”
sentences.n: Two matched sentences, the gentleman and the small man crossed: 不可…而可… 'cannot… but can…'. In 小知 'be known through small things' and 大受 'take on great things', 小 and 大 stand before the verbs as adverbs, 'in a small way', 'in a great way'. 知 is zhī 'to know' here, not the zhì 'understanding' of 15.32. Zhu Xi: this speaks of how to observe people; 知 is my knowing him, 受 is what he takes on (知我知之也受彼所受也). The gentleman in small matters may not be much to look at, but his talent and virtue are enough to bear a heavy charge; the small man, though narrow and shallow in capacity, may still have some one strength worth taking (小人雖器量淺狹而未必無一長可取). He Yan's own comment: the gentleman's way is deep and far, so he cannot be fully known through small things but can take on great ones; the small man's way is shallow and near, so he can be fully known through small things but cannot take on great ones. Variant: He Yan's text adds 也 after the small man's 大受 (不可大受也而可小知也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
民之於仁也，
甚於水火。
水火，吾見蹈而死者矣，
未見蹈仁而死者也。」

morph.gloss: (joins 'the people' and 'toward humaneness' into one topic phrase)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The people, toward humaneness —
it is more than toward water and fire.
Water and fire: I have seen men tread on them and die;
I have never seen one who trod on humaneness and died.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “People need humaneness more than they need water and fire. I have known men walk into water or fire and perish; I have never known anyone perish for walking into humaneness.”
sentences.n: 民之於仁也 'the people in relation to humaneness': 之 sets 民 and 於仁 together as one topic phrase, as 吾之於人也 in 15.24. 甚於 'more than': 於 here marks the comparison. The line does not say more in what; Zhu Xi and Ma Rong both take it as the people's dependence. 水火 'water and fire' is fronted as the topic of the second sentence. 見 jiàn 'to see'; 蹈 dǎo 'to tread on, to step into'; 者 'those who'; 未見 'have never yet seen'. Zhu Xi: the people depend on water and fire to live and cannot do without them for a day, and so it is with humaneness. But water and fire are outside things, while humaneness is in oneself; to lack water and fire harms only the body, while to lack humaneness is to lose one's heart — so humaneness goes beyond water and fire, and is still less to be done without for a day. Besides, water and fire sometimes kill, while humaneness has never killed anyone — why shrink from practising it? He quotes a Mr Li (李氏): these are the Master's words urging people to practise humaneness, and the next chapter is of the same kind. Ma Rong in He Yan: water, fire and humaneness are all things the people look to for life, and humaneness most of all (仁最爲甚也); treading on water or fire sometimes kills, treading on humaneness never yet killed anyone.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
當仁，
不讓於師。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Facing humaneness,
one does not yield to one's teacher.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Where humaneness is at stake, do not hold back, even for your teacher.”
sentences.n: 當 dāng 'to face, to stand at': 當仁 'when it is humaneness (that is in question)'. 讓 ràng 'to yield, to give way', the courtesy of letting another go first; 於師 'to (one's) teacher'. Zhu Xi: 當仁 is taking humaneness as one's own charge (以仁為己任也, echoing 8.7 仁以為己任); even to one's teacher one gives no way — one should go forward boldly and surely do it, for humaneness is what a man has in himself and does himself; there is no contending in it, so what giving way could there be? He quotes Master Cheng: practising humaneness lies with oneself, and there is no one to give way to; were it a good name, which lies outside, one could not but give way (若善名在外則不可不遜). Kong Anguo in He Yan says much the same, and ends: practising humaneness is urgent (行仁急也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子貞而不諒。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l: The Master said: “The gentleman is upright and firm, but not bound by petty good faith.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman holds fast to what is right; he does not cling to his word for its own sake.”
sentences.n: A而不B again, as 15.21: a virtue, and the fault it is kept from. 貞 zhēn: Zhu Xi, 'correct and firm' (貞正而固也). 諒 liàng is 14.18's 'petty good faith'; here Zhu Xi says 諒 is insisting on keeping one's word without choosing between right and wrong (諒則不擇是非而必於信). So the gentleman's firmness holds to what is right, not to whatever he once said; compare 13.20, where 'his words sure to be kept' marks a lesser kind of officer. Kong Anguo in He Yan: 貞 is 'upright', 諒 is 'good faith' (貞正也諒信也); the gentleman keeps his way upright, and his words need not be held to (言不必信也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
事君，
敬其事而後其食。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Serving the lord:
be reverent in the work, and put the salary last.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When you serve a lord, give your whole care to the work and think of the pay only afterwards.”
sentences.n: 事君 'serving the lord' is the topic; then two verbs with their objects, 敬其事 'treat the work with reverence' and 後其食 'put the salary last'. 後 'after' is used as a verb, 'to put after': Zhu Xi says it is the 後 of 後獲 (6.20 先難而後獲, 'puts the hard part first and the gain last'). 食 shí 'what one eats', here the stipend (Zhu Xi: 食禄也). 其 'its' — the work and the pay that belong to the service. Zhu Xi: when the gentleman serves, if he has a post to keep he attends to its duties, if he has the duty of speaking he gives it all his wholeheartedness; in every case he simply treats his own work with reverence, and must not have a mind to seek salary first (不可先有求禄之心也). Kong Anguo in He Yan: first give all one's strength, then eat the salary (先盡力然後食禄也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
有教無類。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Where there is teaching, there are no kinds.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Once there is teaching, it no longer matters what sort a man was to begin with.”
sentences.n: Four characters, two bare clauses: 有教 'there is teaching', 無類 'there are no kinds'. 教 jiào 'to teach, teaching'; 類 lèi 'a kind, a class, a sort'. There is no joining word; how the two clauses relate, the reader supplies. Zhu Xi: human nature is good in all, and that men's kinds differ as good and bad comes from the staining of temperament and habit; so where the gentleman teaches, all can return to the good, and one should no longer speak of the badness of their kind (不當復論其類之惡矣). Ma Rong in He Yan: where people are taught, there are no classes or kinds among them (言人在見教無有種類也).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
道不同，
不相為謀。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Ways not the same —
no planning on each other's behalf.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Men whose ways are not the same have nothing to plan on each other's behalf.”
sentences.n: 道 dào is here a man's way, the course he follows, not only 'the Way'. 相 xiāng 'one another'; 為 wèi 'for, on behalf of' (Zhu Xi: 為去聲); 謀 'to lay plans'. 相為謀 is 'to plan for one another'; the subject, the men whose ways differ, is left unstated. Zhu Xi: 'not the same' means such differences as good and bad, crooked and straight (不同如善惡邪正之類). He Yan has no comment on the chapter.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
辭達而已矣。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Words: they get through, and that is all.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Words are for carrying the meaning through, and nothing more.”
sentences.n: 辭 cí 'words, a speech, the way a thing is put'; 達 dá 'to get through, to reach' (as 12.20); 而已矣 'and that is all' (as 4.15). Zhu Xi: in words, take getting the meaning across and stop there; do not count richness and ornament as skill (辭取達意而止不以富麗為工). He Yan's own comment: if words get through, that is enough; there is no call for ornate words (辭達則足矣不煩文艶之辭也).

sentences.t:
師冕見，
及階，子曰：「階也。」
及席，子曰：「席也。」
皆坐，子告之曰：「
某在斯，
某在斯。」
sentences.l:
Music Master Mian came to see (the Master).
When he reached the steps, the Master said: “The steps.”
When he reached the mat, the Master said: “The mat.”
When all were seated, the Master told him, saying:
“So-and-so is here,
so-and-so is here.”
sentences.i: Mian, the blind music master, came to see the Master. When he reached the steps the Master said, “These are the steps.” When he reached his mat the Master said, “This is your mat.” When everyone was seated, the Master told him who was there: “So-and-so is here, and so-and-so is here.”
sentences.n: 師冕 shī miǎn: 師 is the title 'music master' (as 師摯 in 8.15) and 冕 his name; Zhu Xi: the music master, a blind man, named Mian (師樂師瞽者冕名), and Kong Anguo in He Yan says the same (師樂人盲者也名冕也). Court musicians were, by tradition, blind men. 見 xiàn 'to come to see, to present oneself' (Zhu Xi: 賢遍反). 及 'to reach'; 階 jiē 'the steps' up to the hall; 席 xí 'the mat' one sat on. 階也 and 席也 are whole sentences, a noun and 也: '(these are) the steps'. 皆坐 'all were seated'; 告之 'told him'. 某 mǒu 'so-and-so' stands for each name the Master gave; 斯 'here'. Zhu Xi: saying 'so-and-so is here' twice means he named in turn everyone in their seats to tell him (歷舉在坐之人以詔之); Kong Anguo: he told him in turn the names of those seated and where each was. Variant: He Yan's text reads 及席也, with an extra 也 after 及席, probably a slip of the copy.

sentences.t:
師冕出。
子張問曰：「
與師言之道與？」

morph.gloss: the ceremonial cap (Zhu Xi: 冕，冠也, worn with the apron 黻 as sacrificial dress)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Music Master Mian went out.
Zizhang asked, saying: “Is that the way to speak with a music master?”
sentences.i: When Music Master Mian had gone, Zizhang asked: “Is that the way to talk to a music master?”
sentences.n: 子張 Zizhang is the disciple Zhuansun Shi 顓孫師 (2.18). 與師言 'speaking with a music master' (與 yǔ 'with'), and 之道 'the way of' it: 與師言之道 'the way of speaking with a music master'. The closing 與 is the question particle yú, asking for confirmation, 'is it…?' — Zhu Xi's sound note 與平聲 belongs to it. Zhu Xi: the learners of the sage's school kept in mind and examined every word and every act of the Master, as this shows (聖門學者於夫子之一言一動無不存心省察如此).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
然。
固相師之道也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “It is.
It is certainly the way to assist a music master.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It is. With a blind music master, that is exactly the help one gives.”
sentences.n: 然 'so, it is so', a one-word yes. 固 'certainly, indeed'. 相 xiàng 'to assist' (Zhu Xi: 相去聲 and 相助也); 相師之道 'the way of assisting a (blind) music master'. Zhu Xi: in old times a blind man always had an assistant (古者瞽必有相), and this was the way of it; the sage was not acting with design here, he simply did fully what the way required. He quotes Yin Tun: the sage has one heart in how he conducts himself and how he treats others, and in everything gives his whole sincerity; whoever has a will to learn and seeks the sage's heart can see it here. And Fan Zuyu: the sage does not slight widowers and widows nor ill-treat those with no one to turn to (不侮鰥寡不虐無告), as can be seen here; extend it to the whole world and not one thing would fail to find its place. Ma Rong in He Yan takes 相 as 'to guide' (相導也).
